text: The Lincoln Award for Teaching Programme Handbook 8th June – 12th June 2026 Handbook & Learning Journal For those of you considering a career in teaching, this is the perfect opportunity to gain some experience of different teaching environments. There are a variety of tasks you will be asked to complete during the course of this programme. These are detailed in this handbook. The final day of the programme will provide an exciting opportunity for participants to share their successes through delivery of team presentations. The purpose of this handbook is to ensure: reflection on your experiences ensure focus during observation of lessons development of skills for teaching evaluative and reflective notes that will feed into your celebration presentation We also hope that the completion of this handbook will provide you with an interesting evidence base to support your potential future interviews for teacher training positions. Lincoln Award - Teaching Overview Day Activity Venue Ongoing across the week: as you work with individuals and small groups, reflect on the impact that you have and how you have supported learners (see section 1). Complete a minimum of four reflections of the support you gave and its effectiveness, across the week. Monday, 8th June SETTLING IN: today, get used to the routines of the classroom and start to make relationships with the class(es). See section 2 for ideas on how to develop relationships and reflect on how successful you were. Also, in section 2 take note of key routines across the day; reflect on what these are and the impact of them. Host school, Priory Pembroke Tuesday, 9th June OBSERVATION & SUPPORT DAY Observation of two lessons with some opportunities to support pupils and the teacher (act as an informal Teaching Assistant). Complete section 3 of the handbook to capture your learning notes from your observations. Host school, Priory Pembroke Wednesday, 10th June OBSERVATION & SUPPORT DAY Observation of two lessons with some opportunities to support pupils and the teacher (act as an informal Teaching Assistant). Complete section 4 of the handbook to capture your learning notes from your observations. In readiness for tomorrow: Discuss a possible section of a lesson for you to teach, that will be planned by the class teacher. Choose a lesson that you feel confident to teach – just teach a small section to have a go! Host school, Priory Pembroke Thursday, 11th June OBSERVATION, SUPPORT & A SHORT LESSON INPUT DAY (optional) If you feel comfortable to, teach a section of a lesson. The teacher will plan the lesson and will talk you through what to do/say and why. Discuss the lesson with the teacher and ask them to ‘model’ to you how they would teach it, so you can replicate what they say/do. After the lesson complete section 5 to reflect on your experience. Host school, Priory Pembroke Friday, 12th June Programme Review, Project Presentation & Celebration Day Morning session, from 09:30 until 13:00. In readiness for today, participants need to complete section 6 before the day to evaluate the programme. Participants will work as part of a team to construct a short presentation to communicate their professional learning during their time on the Lincoln Award Programme. Presentations can be in any preferred format - PowerPoint, flip charts, posters etc. Written reports/photographic, evidence/data, etc. might be included to form part of this presentation. You should plan for presentation delivery to take around 10 minutes. The team presentation will be shared, and you will be assessed for your individual contribution.  You will be scored using the Lincoln Award criteria and you will receive your result and feedback within the following week. Upon successful completion of the award, you will receive a digital badge and certificate - full details of this will be provided. University of Lincoln Room MB1010 Section 1: One to One and Small Group Support Record – ongoing throughout the week Throughout the week, the class teacher will ask you to work with individual children and also small groups. Record below these instances (four as a minimum across the week) and reflect on the impact you had. What did you do to support these learners? Did you follow the teacher’s directions? Can you understand why you needed to support the learners in the way that you were directed? Support instance 1 What did you have to do to support the learner(s)? What impact did this have? What did the child/children find hard? How did you help them overcome this? What strategies did you use to support the child/children to understand? Reflection: Monday Period 5, Year 7 Set 1 Mathematics Struggles with multi-step time conversion in speed/distance/time problems. Scaffolded question -> finished worksheet Support instance 2 What did you have to do to support the learner(s)? What impact did this have? What did the child/children find hard? How did you help them overcome this? What strategies did you use to support the child/children to understand? Reflection: Tuesday Period 1, Year 7 Set 3 Mathematics Misconceptions about time conversion (1 hour 45 minutes is not 1.45 hours). Corrected -> finished worksheet. Support instance 3 What did you have to do to support the learner(s)? What impact did this have? What did the child/children find hard? How did you help them overcome this? What strategies did you use to support the child/children to understand? Reflection: Tuesday Period 2, Year 8 Set 1 Mathematics A couple of instances in this lesson with various students having a lack of concentration, so just sitting with the students and gently nudging their focus back when needed. Also clarifying minor bits when they get stuck. Support instance 4 What did you have to do to support the learner(s)? What impact did this have? What did the child/children find hard? How did you help them overcome this? What strategies did you use to support the child/children to understand? Reflection: Tuesday Period 4, Year 9 Set 3 Mathematics Large incident in class – bullying and book throwing. Helped step in when groups were ignoring the teacher and talking afterwards and helped change topic if it was brought up again after resolution. Helped with angle measurement, afterwards: students kept reading the wrong scale, helped clarify that they must follow the direction of the curve inside of the angle, on the protractor. Multiple students then got 100% on worksheets after this adjustment. Support instance 5+ While more support was given after Tuesday, I mostly finished the booklet by this point so focused more on getting as much experience as possible and just reflecting at the end – brief notes were kept in my personal journal, too. Copy and paste more cells below according to have many times you want to reflect on the support you have given – 4 is the minimum expectation. Section 2: Getting to Know you! Monday 8th June Relationships are at the heart of being a good teacher, so spend today getting to know the children and their names. Also, get used to the routines within the school; focus and reflect on these two key elements today be completing the sections below – using the scaffolds as a support. Suggested ways to make relationships with children: Have a smile on your face – this makes such a difference! Stand with confidence; don’t let them know you are nervous even if you are Introduce yourself: use Mr/Miss/Ms/Mrs and then surname – no Christian names Get down to their level to speak to them; leaning over a child can be intimidating Learn their names – maybe take in card and ask them to put their name on the card at the start of the day/lesson? Ask about themselves – what are their hobbies and interests? Keep it professional – don’t use phrases like ‘mate’; you aren’t their friend Set clear boundaries to gain respect; if they start to become over familiar step back Volunteer to help them; don’t sit in the corner waiting to be directed – get stuck in and offer to help the children Read the schools vision/values and behaviour policy before you go in – ask the teacher if you can give out rewards and ensure you are following school policy. Check with the teacher if you feel a behavior is unsuitable; don’t put yourself in a vulnerable situation Stay with your class teacher all day and observe how they talk to the children and the language/phrases they use Reflection on how I made positive relationships today: (use some of the scaffolds above as a prompt as you write) Introduced myself at the beginning of each lesson, if I saw the class for the first time. Students then got curious and instigated conversation with me – during minor tasks like handing out stationary, they’d ask questions and I’d do so back to learn more about each individual’s hobbies/interests. Clarified behaviour expectations with each teacher before the lesson, including asking if there’s anything they’d like me to help with (or specific groups to watch out for, etc.). How I aim to build on this tomorrow: Instigate more conversations by myself with the students. Routines are central to the successful running of a classroom/lesson. Use the prompts below to help you consider the impact of routines: What are the routines of the school day? What are the specific timings that need to be considered? Are there any routines for when the children enter and leave the room? Are there any routines/expectations for what the children do once they have sat down at the start of the day/lesson? Are there any routines for questions and answers? What are the routines/expectations for partner and group work? What are the routines for working independently? Are there routines at the end of the lesson – what are the expectations for packing away and finishing the learning? Are there particular routines within the different subjects? Reflection on how routines were used today and their impact in managing a classroom: (use some of the scaffolds above as a prompt as you write) Starter on the board as soon as students enter, and they’re expected to work on them immediately. Answers are then discussed as soon as everyone is settled. Teacher explains the topic through an “I do/You do” structure – they explain how to do a few examples, leaving key parts on the board, then the students collaboratively solve an example (hands up contributions), then complete a short worksheet independently as the teacher (and me!) walks around to help. Each lesson ends differently depending on the teacher, but almost always a short game of sorts. Maybe a form of Countdown, or a quick anagram game for “Language for Learning”, each with sweet rewards or early breaks. How will you use your understanding of routines to support you for the rest of the week? To know when to step in to help the teachers do miscellaneous tasks like handing out stationary, as well as when to step in and help students learn/understand. Section 3: Observation and Support Day Tuesday 9th June Observe a minimum of two lessons in detail today; the rest of the day support and become familiar with the class routines/school expectations. Use the proforma to include reflections on both lessons – use the prompts on the left-hand side to focus your thinking. Focus area Observations (what strategies are used and what impact do they have?) Questions you may have (to reflect on throughout the session) Behaviour for Learning Strategies Observed How does the teacher foster respectful relationships? How do they set boundaries and high expectations? What strategies do they use to manage behavior? Lots of smiles, greetings, and personal follow-ups for students to catch up and show interest. However, all while maintaining hard discipline if any rules are broken or boundaries crossed, as well as avoiding/ignoring more personal questions entirely. Let the students have “brain breaks”, or even let them release energy after completing questions (or giving space) for SEN students. Start of the lesson How does the teacher recap and revisit prior learning? Why do you think they do this? Starters to reinforce previous learning, as well as recent misconceptions or failed questions. This is to help fix these misconceptions over time (spaced repetition with low cognitive load), as well as give the students a quick win to start the lesson with. How are pupils engaged and encouraged to participate in the lesson/learning? What strategies are used to encourage participation? How are children managed who don’t engage/participate? Sweets and early breaks towards the end of lessons, but otherwise house points: courage points, wisdom points, or behaviour points. The less engaged students are often picked on during questions or sat down with one-to-one while completing worksheets. Some even have TAs with them, asking/answering questions for them too, especially for the SEN students. Structure of the Main Body of the lesson How is learning broken down into manageable chunks? Why does the teach do this? How does the teacher make clear what they want the learning to look like? Why do they ‘think aloud’? How do they ‘model’ the learning and expectations to the children? Learning is broken down using scaffolding to be more digestible and reduce cognitive load for the students. They perform an example themselves, to show what the learning should be like, saying the steps aloud to really point out every part of the methods/reasoning – as well as possible misconceptions. This is all part of the “I do/You do” method used throughout the school, enforced by the headteacher. Supporting learners needs How are children challenged in the lesson? If children are struggling, how are they supported? How does the teacher ensure all understand the learning and can achieve in the lesson? Extension tasks are built in to the lessons for everyone to complete, but these are always open-ended (like working through a textbook) so that each student can work to as much challenge as they can cope with. If anyone is struggling, then they’re helped individually. For the SEN children, they’re often left alone if needed and guided towards “their people” so they can settle down. Someone mentioned “Axiom” as a mathematics club for higher-achievers, I’m interested in what it’s about! (I later found out that it’s about solving puzzles etc., also an interesting career path!) How learning and progress is assessed through the lesson How does the teacher know if the children understand or not? How do they work out who doesn’t understand the learning and who needs help? How does the teacher provide instant feedback on the learning? Asking spot-check/cold-call questions, formative assessments (worksheets), and end of unit mini tests (assessment for learning). For instant feedback, they often use peer assessment – also to reduce teacher workload. The plenary/review and lesson close How does the lesson finish? How does the teacher know if the learning was achieved or not? What strategies do they use to summarise the learning? Language for learning anagrams, plus sweet/point rewards. Spot checks while students leave (waiting for the bell), making the students summarise the class learning. Complete the one-to-one and small group activity record (minimum of two a day) Section 4: Observation and Support Day Wednesday 10th June Observe a minimum of two different lessons in detail today; the rest of the day support and become familiar with the class routines/school expectations. Use the proforma to include reflections on both lessons – use the prompts on the left-hand side to focus your thinking. Focus area Observations (what strategies are used and what impact do they have?) Questions you may have (to reflect on throughout the session) Behaviour for Learning Strategies Observed How does the teacher foster respectful relationships? How do they set boundaries and high expectations? What strategies do they use to manage behavior? Asking questions about the students, apologising for any mistakes made – even making mistakes on purpose to point out common ones, and reward the students for any corrections made. Feigning ignorance on topics/behaviour also always the teacher to be more level with the students while managing behaviour expectations. Seating plans are often used to manage behaviour, starting strict and then becoming more lenient over time to reduce conflict (rather than imposing them afterwards). How are seating plans first decided? Start of the lesson How does the teacher recap and revisit prior learning? Why do you think they do this? Starters to reinforce previous learning, as well as recent misconceptions or failed questions. This is to help fix these misconceptions over time (spaced repetition with low cognitive load), as well as give the students a quick win to start the lesson with. How are pupils engaged and encouraged to participate in the lesson/learning? What strategies are used to encourage participation? How are children managed who don’t engage/participate? Spot-checks and cold-calling, for questions but also to just reassure students that they’re correct if nervous (giving easier questions), quickly moving on if any mistakes are made. If any students can’t get to the answer when chosen, the teacher scaffolds them towards the answer by breaking it up, or gets other students to help out. Send out anxious students during telling off so that they’re not punished for no reason. Follow the pace of the slowest student, or at least giving them one-to-one support if needed. Section 5: Teaching a Section of a Lesson Thursday 11th June Depending on your confidence; have a go at teaching a section from a lesson today. Agree this with the class teacher the day before, so you have time to consider what you will say/do. Ask the teacher to ‘model’ to you and show you what to do/say and then you ‘practise’ having a go. If you choose not to teach whole class, have a go at teaching a small group and modelling to them instead. Describe what you taught? Compound shapes and how to calculate their area. Was there any subject specific vocabulary that you had to use? Some standard vocab like “area” and “formula”, as well as specific shape names and properties. How did you manage behaviour as you taught? Was this successful? Why? Talking directly to students if they appear to be distracted, talking, or misbehaving, so that they immediately must engage again. This often meant bouncing around the room, which in turn led to more engagement as everyone had to be slightly on edge and energetic. This worked, as everyone began to focus more as I talked more, rather than initial period of slight chatter in the back. Did the children understand what you taught – how do you know? Yes, as during one-to-ones afterwards then they all had correct answers in worksheets, and some students even thanked me for helping them finally understand – that it was “actually really easy”. What was successful about your teaching? Everyone understood the topic, at least for that hour. If you were to teach that again, what would you change and why? Larger group to test my behaviour management more – it’s definitely the weakest aspect of my teaching with the school environment. Section 6: Lincoln Award for Teaching – Participant Programme Evaluation Please complete at the end of the week, in time for our meeting on Friday 12th June Summarise how you feel at the close of your Lincoln Award for teaching Internship Programme. I’m very thankful for the opportunity, and it’s been very insightful to view things from the teacher’s perspective – their façade of ignorance while jotting down behaviour, or how they act after telling off a classroom. What do you feel have been your key successes across the week? Why? I’ve seen a huge amount in such a small period of time, and I’m definitely proud of my engagement with the students and personal development realising that they welcome my presence and input. Where are your areas for development? Are there ways you can continue your links with the school to develop in these areas? Involving myself more with the students, instigating the help rather than waiting for someone to put their hand up or start misbehaving. I’m been offered a chance to come back, too, so I look forward to discussing that further and exploring the pastoral side of the school more, perhaps. Is teaching the route for you? Did you choose the right phase/age range? I think secondary is the correct age range if were to teach, although I definitely need more experience before making the decision. I’d also like to explore “Axiom” more before committing, too, as well as the potential of teaching computer science on top of the mathematics. Is there anything that we (providers and university) could have done better? Better communication with the school – they didn’t know much about why I was there, or what I had to do. Any other points you would like to share with us It was incredibly interesting and I learned so much, even just about the state of education and students at the moment. I’m truly grateful! I made many more notes in my personal journal, as well as on the actual hard copy of this, but even just these highlights have been amazing to learn and write about. Thank you so much for your taking part in the scheme. We hope to hear from you in the future – please contact Lincolnshire ITT for further support and advice on: scittenquiries@prioryacademies.co.uk
